*Chamath says reinstating Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO would undermine corporate governance and put the company at risk, despite Huang's extraordinary track record. Speaking on the All-In Podcast, Chamath argued that unresolved questions surrounding Huang's conduct make a return untenable.*

• *Governance Risks:* Chamath argues that reinstating Huang amid unresolved controversies and substantial shareholder losses would undermine Nvidia *($NVDA)* governance standards and expose the company and its stakeholders to further risks.
• *Huang's Legacy:* Chamath described Huang as an exceptional, legendary founder who built one of the world's most important companies, but emphasized that the full extent of his mistakes remains unknown.
• *Reinstatement Outlook:* Chamath believes Huang will not return and that Nvidia's board must maintain its position against reinstatement to preserve corporate governance and credibility.
• *Interim CEO:* Chamath praised Colette Kress, calling her excellent, but said she has been placed in the difficult position of communicating the board's decisions while absorbing public criticism.
• *Employee Backlash:* Chamath criticized online attacks against Kress, arguing that she is delivering the board's message and should not be blamed for its decision.
FBI'S NATIONAL CRIME INFORMATION CENTER HACKED -CNN

*The FBI is investigating an apparent cyber breach targeting its National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a critical database used by law enforcement nationwide to access criminal records and warrants, CNN reports, citing two people briefed on the investigation. The incident marks the bureau's second reported major cybersecurity breach in recent months.*

• *Crime Database Targeted:* Hackers reportedly targeted NCIC, a system connecting federal, state and local law enforcement agencies. The FBI discovered the suspected intrusion in recent days and is investigating its extent.
• *Critical Law Enforcement Data:* NCIC contains information on wanted and missing persons, arrest warrants, protection orders, registered sex offenders, stolen vehicles and firearms. Officers rely on the system for real-time information during investigations and traffic stops.
• *Potential Exposure:* The attackers' identities, method of entry and extent of access remain unknown. Authorities have not confirmed whether criminal records were stolen, altered or compromised, or whether the system's operations were disrupted.
• *Previous FBI Breach:* In September, the ShinyHunters hacking group targeted the FBI's employment website, exposing sensitive employee information. A Canadian cybersecurity executive was subsequently arrested in connection with that investigation.
• *Wider Cybersecurity Concerns:* The reported intrusion follows high-profile disruptions affecting U.S. banks, the NSA and FAA systems. No connection between those incidents and the suspected FBI breach has been established.

*The Financial Times traced an alleged Nvidia AI chip-smuggling network tied to former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang and a man U.S. authorities describe as a leader of Cambodia’s Prince Group.*

U.S. investigators are examining whether Megaspeed, which the FT describes as Nvidia’s largest Southeast Asian customer, helped divert chips to China. Alice Huang was reportedly romantically involved with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Some U.S. officials suspect she was a Chinese spy. Beijing called that allegation a “smear.”

• *U.S. supplier* Washington put China’s Inspur on its export blacklist in March 2023 over alleged military ties. Its part-owned California unit, renamed Aivres, stayed off the list and kept trading with Nvidia. Nvidia questioned the Inspur link internally but concluded Aivres met compliance and export-control requirements.
• *How Megaspeed qualified* The FT says people tied to gaming group Century Huatong helped set up Megaspeed using an offshore gaming company’s Singapore unit, which Alice Huang bought and renamed in 2023. The unit had years of corporate records. Megaspeed passed Nvidia’s checks after pitching Malaysian data centers and a leasing contract with Alibaba. Huang’s husband, Kang Wei, was an early Century Huatong investor whose fund backed a data center project involving both gaming firms.
• *Cambodia link* FT sources say Hu Xiaowei helped move chips into China. U.S. authorities describe Hu, who was arrested in Japan, as Prince Group’s second-in-command. Corporate records link him to Century Huatong through a gaming company controlled by its chair. Another director had business ties to Fang Zhizhen, whom the U.S. sanctioned over alleged money laundering for Prince Group. Prince Group said Hu never worked for it, disputed any connection to Fang and denied operating an illicit network.
• *Shipments* A Malaysian Megaspeed subsidiary declared about $4.6B in goods imported from Aivres from December 2024 through December 2025, according to trade records. FT sources say many of the chips reached China. Separately, The Straits Times reported that Indonesian police found server racks without GPUs at a local Megaspeed subsidiary in early 2026.
• *China distribution* FT sources identify Shanghai Century Litong as a key distributor of smuggled chips, which sold for multiples of their original price. Litong was founded by a joint venture between Century Huatong and an investment vehicle controlled by Alice Huang and her sister. Bloomberg reported that restricted Nvidia chips were found at data centers linked to that venture.
• *Tencent and Alibaba* Both have business ties to Century Huatong, and Tencent owns 10.1%. The FT found no evidence either company participated in chip smuggling. Tencent said it had no connection to or knowledge of the alleged activity. Alibaba did not respond.
• *Export controls* The FT previously reported at least $1B in smuggled Nvidia chips sold in China in three months after the U.S. tightened H20 restrictions. The Trump administration announced further limits on access through Southeast Asia this week. Georgetown researcher Hanna Dohmen said strong unmet demand could push smuggling to other countries.

*FT maps Alice Huang’s ties to alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips into China*

U.S. authorities are investigating whether Megaspeed, where Huang was an executive, helped divert the chips. The FT graphic traces the sales, investments and board ties around the alleged network.

• *1. Family investments* Alice Huang and her family invested in projects with Century Huatong. One venture, Century Longteng, founded Century Litong, which FT sources say distributed smuggled chips in China.
• *2. Chip supplier* Aivres, Inspur’s U.S. unit, sold Nvidia products to Speedmatrix, Megaspeed’s Malaysian subsidiary.
• *3. Gaming ties* Century Huatong chair Wang Ji’s holdings linked him to gaming firm 7Road and gave him an indirect majority stake in Zhenao Network.
• *4. Cambodia link* Hu Xiaowei sat on Zhenao’s board. U.S. authorities allege Hu was second-in-command at Cambodia’s Prince Group and Fang Zhizhen laundered money for it. Prince Group says Hu never worked for it and disputes any link to Fang.

Scott Bessent struck a softer tone on U.S.-China chip restrictions, one week after criticizing Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over Nvidia *($NVDA)* export controls. Bessent now says existing restrictions are sufficient, reiterating that Washington seeks to "de-risk, not decouple" from China.

• *Export Policy:* Bessent said appropriate chip restrictions are in place and Chinese access to advanced U.S. computing through overseas data centers has been curtailed. He expects no further changes to Nvidia's H200 export policy.
• *Nvidia Shipments:* Bessent said Nvidia stopped shipping H200 chips to China despite previously receiving U.S. export approvals, citing weak Chinese demand.
• *Lutnick Dispute:* On November 13, Bessent said Treasury, Defense, State and the U.S. Trade Representative had supported blacklisting Nvidia customer Megaspeed for months, but Commerce controlled the decision. Asked Friday about the dispute, he emphasized that officials follow Trump's instructions.
• *China Strategy:* Bessent rejected being labeled a hawk or dove, emphasizing the importance of maintaining economic ties while reducing strategic risks. He highlighted Trump's third meeting with President Xi Jinping this year and a fourth planned at the G20 in Doral.
• *Policy Distinction:* Bessent's comments signal a softer public approach toward the Commerce dispute, not a reversal of his broader China strategy. He previously supported "de-risking, not decoupling."

All-In Podcast host David Friedberg says the circumstances surrounding Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia *($NVDA)* remain unclear, arguing that investors lack a complete factual account of allegations involving espionage, chip exports and executive misconduct.

• *Unanswered Questions:* Friedberg says it remains uncertain whether Huang's departure stemmed from concerns over chip sales to China, potential espionage, personal relationships or violations of corporate conduct policies.
• *Media Scrutiny:* Friedberg questioned the reliability of competing reports, arguing that insufficient firsthand evidence has been disclosed to determine which allegations are accurate.
• *Official Disclosures:* Nvidia confirmed Huang's resignation, cited conduct inconsistent with company standards and launched an independent investigation. However, it has not publicly released the findings or provided a complete account of the events.
• *Legal Scrutiny:* Friedberg emphasized the absence of publicly announced government charges establishing wrongdoing. Separately, shareholders have filed lawsuits alleging misleading disclosures and inadequate oversight, while Reuters reports an SEC investigation into potential accounting issues.
• *Investor Uncertainty:* Friedberg argues that without fuller disclosures from Nvidia, Huang and government authorities, investors cannot reliably distinguish established facts from allegations and speculation.

*Amazon is in advanced talks to buy AI startup Decart for about $7.5B, according to people familiar with the matter.* A deal could come together as soon as early next week, though talks could still fall apart. The Wall Street Journal previously reported the talks.

• *Why AWS wants it* Decart’s software frees up chip capacity by running AI models more efficiently. Decart was an early user of Amazon’s Trainium3 chip, which launched in late 2025 to compete with Nvidia’s GPUs.
• *Decart’s valuation* Three Israeli engineers founded Decart in 2023. It was valued at $4B in May after raising $300M from investors including Nvidia, Radical Ventures, Sequoia Capital and Benchmark. Its Lucy and Oasis products let users edit video live and generate interactive virtual worlds.
• *Deal size* Amazon agreed to buy satellite operator Globalstar for $11.5B earlier this year and paid $8.4B for MGM in 2022.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung urged faster AI infrastructure development Saturday while visiting SK Group's $5.2 billion data center project with Amazon Web Services *($AMZN)* in Ulsan. Lee warned that speed is critical in the global AI race and called for greater investment, regional expansion and workforce development.

• *$5.2B AI Investment:* SK Group and AWS are jointly developing the Ulsan facility, with approximately 7 trillion won ($5.2B) in planned investment through 2029. Initial operations are scheduled for the second half of 2027.
• *Gigawatt Expansion:* The project targets an initial 103 MW of capacity by 2029, with plans to add nearly 900 MW over time, potentially bringing the facility close to 1 GW.
• *AI Chip Demand:* Lee emphasized that data centers are a major driver of semiconductor demand and said the project's success could attract additional investment from global AI companies. SK Group is pursuing further technology partnerships.
• *Regional Development:* Lee highlighted the need to expand AI investment beyond Seoul, positioning Ulsan as an example of how large-scale infrastructure projects can support regional economic growth.
• *Labor Shortages:* Approximately 900 workers are employed at the construction site. Lee warned that advanced infrastructure projects face construction labor shortages and urged government ministries to expand workforce training.

*Taiwan imposed its first market-wide short-selling restrictions in 11 years after its benchmark Taiex plunged a record 17.5% this week, as the global AI selloff battered semiconductor stocks. The emergency measures take effect Monday, November 23, and aim to stabilize markets following three rounds of intervention this month.*

• *Historic Market Collapse:* The Taiex plunged 6.23% Friday to 36,033.29, its lowest close in nearly seven months and third-largest daily point decline on record. The index lost 7,641.83 points this week, its biggest weekly decline ever.
• *Short-Selling Restrictions:* Starting Monday, investors cannot execute short sales below the previous session's closing price across all listed and OTC stocks and Taiwan Depositary Receipts. Securities firms and futures companies conducting qualifying hedging transactions are exempt.
• *Higher Margin Requirements:* Regulators raised minimum short-selling collateral requirements from 130% to 150% and suspended new applications to list put warrants, limiting bearish trading activity.
• *Additional Market Support:* Authorities encouraged listed companies to repurchase shares and financial institutions to suspend stock lending, recall existing loans early or decline renewals. Taiwan's NT$500B ($15.2B) market stabilization fund has been authorized to intervene since November 6.

Steve Eisman warns the fallout from Jensen Huang's departure at Nvidia *($NVDA)* is only beginning and could become "very ugly" for banks, private credit, private equity, companies and shareholders as the financial consequences unfold.

• *Unwind Accelerating:* Eisman believes the full fallout has yet to emerge, warning that financial institutions, companies and investors must confront potential damage to their balance sheets.
• *Huang's Return:* Eisman says technology leaders recognize the risks and want Huang reinstated, but doubts he could return directly to Nvidia.
• *Treasury Scrutiny:* Eisman characterizes Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent as a self-appointed watchdog, suggesting heightened government scrutiny could complicate Huang's return.
• *Financial Exposure:* Eisman expects banks, private credit firms, private equity investors and shareholders to face potentially significant financial consequences, although he did not quantify the exposure or identify specific institutions.

Tech analyst Dan Ives calls the Friday selloff a "March 2020 COVID moment," describing a perfect storm of Nvidia *($NVDA)* leadership turmoil, China semiconductor restrictions, AI financing concerns and deteriorating market sentiment. Despite the "horror show" on Wall Street, Ives believes the decline is a short-lived bottoming process and maintains his bullish AI outlook into 2027.

• *Perfect Storm:* Ives cited Jensen Huang's departure, Nvidia's governance crisis, China-related semiconductor scrutiny and growing concerns over AI infrastructure spending as major drivers of the tech selloff.
• *Market Pressure:* Forced selling, mounting fund losses and reduced buying power have intensified declines. Ives also cited sticky inflation, hawkish Fed commentary and tighter financial conditions.
• *Anthropic IPO:* Ives called Anthropic's *($ANT)* historic debut a watershed event, but said its subsequent 9% decline deepened investor anxiety. The massive offering may also have temporarily diverted liquidity from other technology stocks.
• *Bottoming Process:* Ives compared the fear gripping technology investors to March 2020, calling the selloff a "white-knuckle moment" but expecting the turbulence to be relatively short-lived.
• *AI Outlook:* Ives maintains that the projected $4 trillion AI infrastructure buildout remains intact and continues backing his long-term technology thesis into 2027, despite near-term volatility.
